projects.label: Reports
projects.title: Built, shipped
projects.intro: The platform’s two main services: an educational roulette and a job-search pipeline. I designed, built and run both myself, from the interface down to the cluster.

roulette.name: Roulette
roulette.what: An educational roulette on grumbles, the platform’s own currency. One round every 30 seconds, live for everyone, and every result checks out in your browser.
roulette.note: The screens show a build with made-up players and a made-up balance.

highlights.term: Fair by a chain of seeds
highlights.text: A chain of a million SHA-256 seeds is built backwards, and its commit is published before the season. The public seed comes from a drand beacon round that has not happened yet, so nobody can pick a convenient chain, me included.
The fairness page runs the same engine code as the server: the hash of the revealed seed and the round’s number are recomputed right on your machine.

highlights.term: The engine doesn’t pick the number
highlights.text: A separate fair-roll service, the only one holding the secret, works it out. The round engine neither picks the result nor knows it in advance.
One replica drives the rounds on a lease in Valkey. Every phase change is a conditional UPDATE keyed by the round number, so a former leader waking up after a pause cannot write over anything.

highlights.term: A bet is never taken twice
highlights.text: A reserve in one Lua script in Valkey, a debit from the wallet by the bet’s key, a batched write to Postgres every 5 ms. The player hears back only after the commit.
A WebSocket opened by a one-time ticket and a full round snapshot 4 times a second: a lost tick breaks nothing, and the strip stops for everyone at once.

table.caption: A round taking bets
table.alt: The roulette on a computer: a round taking bets, the strip resting on the last result, the latest results by it, and below three columns of bets by colour: red ×2, green ×14 and black ×2.

phone.caption: The same round on a phone
phone.alt: The same roulette round on a phone screen: the strip and the latest results.

atelier.name: Atelier
atelier.what: A job-search pipeline: it finds vacancies, scores the fit, builds a tailored LaTeX CV for each one and keeps every application on a board.
atelier.private: Private for now: sign-in is by invitation only.
atelier.note: The screens show the demo mode: a made-up candidate and made-up companies.

highlights.text: Search, reading the vacancy, matching, building the CV, the ATS check, sending: each step is its own task type with its own RabbitMQ queue. Retries after 15 seconds, a minute and five minutes, then a dead-letter queue, so a job never hangs.

highlights.term: A model only where code can’t cope
highlights.text: A model reads the vacancy once, writes the texts and checks them. Picking the cases and skills and fitting the CV to its length is plain code.
llm-gateway puts Codex CLI, Claude CLI and MiniMax behind one API, and Codex runs in a sandbox of its own.
XeLaTeX builds the CV from a template. The board shows the ATS keyword coverage and what changed against the master CV, and the facts come only from a bank of cases.

highlights.term: A real browser for the forms
highlights.text: Chromium driven by Playwright fills in the ATS forms. It never gets round a captcha or a login: such an application is flagged as needing a human.

board.caption: The applications board
board.alt: The atelier’s board: columns for each stage, from vacancies found to applications sent, with the fit score and the vacancy’s source on every card.

cv.caption: A CV tailored to the vacancy
cv.alt: An application opened over the board: the PDF CV built for the vacancy, its ATS keyword coverage and the list of changes against the master CV.

platform.label: Blueprint
platform.title: One platform
platform.intro: The roulette, the atelier, Battleship and the textbooks run on a platform I built and operate. The account, the wallet, notifications, payments and the operator console are shared by every outegro.dev app, all on a single K3s node behind Cloudflare.

items.name: Sign-in
items.result: One account for every app: an email code or Google, active sessions, a security page and Telegram linking.

items.name: Wallet
items.result: Grumbles, the platform’s own currency. Roulette bets and wins and the daily bonus go through it by an operation key, so a retry never counts twice.

items.name: Notifications
items.result: Email and Telegram messages in the user’s language, with billing and security templates.

items.name: Operator console
items.result: Users, roles, payments, notifications, a roulette section and an audit log of operator actions.

items.name: Monitoring
items.result: Metrics and logs from every service, with Telegram alerts for failing pods, expiring certificates, stale backups and stuck queues.

items.name: Delivery
items.result: Every change is linted, type-checked, tested and built. Argo CD rolls it out from Git, and a rollback is a plain revert.

items.name: Data
items.result: PostgreSQL with a database per service, continuous WAL archiving and daily backups to Cloudflare R2. Restoring from backup has been tested for real.

items.name: Messaging
items.result: Events between services go through an outbox and an inbox: none are lost, none are applied twice.

items.name: Cluster
items.result: One K3s node behind Cloudflare. TLS certificates renew on their own, and secrets are sealed in Git.

faq.label: Letters to the editor
faq.title: Your questions,
faq.intro: What people usually ask before we start.

items.q: Who owns the code and the accounts?
items.a: You do, from day one. The repository, the domain, hosting, payment and email services are set up in your name or your company’s, and I work in them as an invited member. All the code and its full history stay in your repository.

The project does not hang on one person. Documentation on the architecture, setup and operations, tests and automated builds are part of the work, not an extra. You hold every access from the start, so your team or another engineer can pick it up. And when we wrap up, I hand the project over and walk your team through it.
Yes. If the task cannot be described without a non-disclosure agreement, send me yours and we sign it before getting into the details.

items.q: How much does it cost, and can I pay in parts?
items.a: It depends on the scope and the format: a project is priced by estimate, long-term work by the month, an audit at a fixed price. Bigger work is split into stages and paid stage by stage, and every stage ends with something you can open and check. We settle the exact amount and the payment schedule after a short call about the task.

items.q: Who makes changes and supports the product after launch?
items.a: We can keep going as long-term work: fixes, improvements, new features and an eye on metrics and alerts. Or your own team takes over, and by then it has everything it needs: the code, documentation, tests and access.
Usually within a day. If you would rather talk, book a call: 30 minutes at a time that suits you.

meta.title: Privacy — Nick Lukashik
meta.description: What data outegro.dev and its apps handle, why, and how you stay in control.

privacy.title: Your data,
privacy.intro: outegro.dev and its apps — the account at id.outegro.dev, payments and future products — are run by Nick Lukashik, an independent engineer. This page explains what data they handle, why, and how you stay in control.

sections.title: What is collected and why
items: Account: your email address, an optional display name and your preferred language — to sign you in and to write to you about your account.

Sign-in and security: one-time codes, stored only as a hash and valid for ten minutes. For each session: browser and operating system, IP address, sign-in time and last activity — to protect the account and to show you where you are signed in.
Notifications: messages in your account inbox, their delivery status and the channels you chose.
Payments, once available: orders and subscription status. Card details are entered on the payment provider’s page and never reach this platform.

This website: reader statistics through Google Analytics, only if you say yes. They show how many people visit, where they come from and which pages they open; your name and email never reach them. No advertising or ad tracking. Server logs with IP addresses are kept for a short time for security and troubleshooting.

sections.title: Cookies
items: og_locale — your language for all outegro.dev sites, kept for one year.

og_at and og_rt — your session in a platform app such as id.outegro.dev, and on outegro.dev itself once you sign in from its header (or automatically, see og_hint). They are HttpOnly, so scripts cannot read them, and live for five minutes and thirty days respectively.

og_hint — a note that this browser is signed in at id.outegro.dev. It is set for the whole .outegro.dev domain, so the other platform sites can let you in without signing in again. It holds no personal data, just “1”; it lives as long as your session at id.outegro.dev and is removed when you sign out.

og_silent — each site’s own note about automatic sign-in: “tried” for five minutes after an attempt (a day if the attempt failed for a reason that would repeat); “silent” while a session opened automatically lives, and that session ends together with your session at id.outegro.dev; “out” for a year after you sign out yourself or a session is revoked, so the site never lets you back in without you.
og_sso — a sign-in in progress: a one-time check and the page to return to. It lives for ten minutes and is deleted as soon as sign-in is complete.
og_gate — a note that you skipped the opening animation (a click or Esc): it stays away until you close the browser.
og_consent — your answer about statistics: granted or denied. Kept for one year, on outegro.dev only.

_ga and _ga_<number> — Google Analytics cookies: a random browser number that ties visits to one reader. They are set only after you say yes, last up to two years from your last visit and are deleted if you change your mind.
Cloudflare, which delivers the sites, may set its own security cookies such as __cf_bm to tell people from bots.
All of these except _ga are needed for the sites to work and need no consent. The site asks about statistics separately, in a note at the bottom of the page.

sections.title: Who else processes data
items: The hosting provider of the server the platform runs on.
Cloudflare — every request passes through its network, which protects the sites from attacks and delivers them; it also runs the domain name system and stores encrypted backups.
Resend — email delivery.
Google — sign-in with Google, only if you choose it. It shares your email address, name and whether the email is verified.

Google — reader statistics for outegro.dev through Google Tag Manager and Google Analytics. The Tag Manager loader comes from Google’s servers on every page but sets no cookies itself; Google Analytics starts only after you say yes. Google Analytics does not store IP addresses, and Google may process the data in the United States and other countries.
Telegram — only if you link it for notifications.
Lava — payment processing, once payments are available.

sections.title: How long it is kept
items: Account data stays until you ask to delete the account.
Sign-in codes expire after ten minutes. Ended sessions and security records are kept for a limited time to investigate misuse.
Google Analytics data tied to a browser number: 14 months, after which only aggregate figures remain.
Your answer about statistics: one year; when it expires, the site asks again.
Backups are encrypted and replaced on a rolling basis.

sections.title: Your choices
items: Change your name and language, end sessions and choose notification channels in your account at id.outegro.dev.

Change your mind about statistics at any time in the statistics settings below. Once you say no, Google Analytics no longer starts and its cookies are deleted. You can also block cookies in your browser or use a content blocker: the site works fine without statistics.
To get a copy of your data or to delete your account, write to the address below. Requests are answered within 30 days.

sections.title: Changes
items: If this policy changes in a meaningful way, signed-in users get a notice in the account inbox before the change takes effect.

column.label: Editor’s column
column.title: How I became
text: Hi, I’m Nick! I’ve been writing code since I was 12. It started with websites for Counter-Strike servers (HTML, CSS, JS, PHP), so headshots have been part of my life for a long time :) From 2016 I was already building Counter-Strike projects to order: roulette and jackpot sites, Steam trade bots, a browser extension with skin prices. Somehow it never stopped.

Now it’s 6+ years of commercial full-stack work, mostly TypeScript, React, Next.js and Node.js with Postgres. I joined my first company in January 2020, before university even started, and then studied at MIREA alongside the job.

Right now I’m at Printify, a big print-on-demand platform, where I work on both the frontend and the APIs. At one point I took a whole B2B ordering product from an idea to production with a small team. That’s the kind of work I like most: you own something end to end and then actually watch people use it. Alongside that I’m an AI full-stack engineer at Toggle, building LLM products: from a self-hosted open-source model on GPUs to RAG and MCP agents.

I’m pretty AI-first in how I work. I use coding agents for most of the code, with my own rules and skills for them, and Jira and Confluence plugged in through MCP. I still review every step myself, because the agent is fast but I’m the one who gets the call when prod breaks :)

For fun I run my own platform, outegro.dev, on a Kubernetes cluster I set up myself. I’m the only DevOps, the on-call and the person who gets paged there. It’s my playground where I try things out before I bring them to work.

I like to keep learning. My favorite way is to take a service I already know well and rewrite it from scratch in something new. Lately that’s been Go and Rust. That’s how my platform’s watchdog got rewritten, and its drawing is in the hobby club below.

incidents.title: What broke
incidents.intro: Tales from production: short notes on what broke on my watch and what was done about it.

notes.title: Minor version runs riot
notes.text: A minor Bun release broke next-auth right in production. Rolling back did not help: the old builds had already been overwritten. The bug was reproduced on dev, Bun went back to the previous version, and later the fix landed upstream.
notes.measures: versions are now pinned like life depends on it.

notes.title: Post-quantum signature too big for the door
notes.text: On Node 24, SimpleWebAuthn offered the ML-DSA-44 algorithm first. Its signature weighs 3.2 KB, and passkey sign-in broke.
notes.measures: passkey registration is pinned to ES256, EdDSA and RS256.

notes.title: Eleven apps go out at once
notes.text: During a full rollout of all 11 apps the server lost its way out to the internet: load average around 68, image pulls failing. Then it all came back by itself.
notes.measures: none, the server caught its breath and went back to work on its own.

notes.title: Load test chokes the home internet
notes.text: A load test ran from home, from one IP, through Cloudflare. Cloudflare started dropping connections, and the home link, about 460 KB/s, filled up completely.
notes.measures: load tests now run on the server itself, straight at the origin.

notes.title: Late webhook rewrites history
notes.text: Messaging webhooks arrived out of order, and a delayed callback overwrote newer CRM state.
notes.measures: events got versions and updates became idempotent. A latecomer can’t overwrite anything now.

notes.title: One slow carrier holds up the whole checkout
notes.text: A single slow delivery provider could hang the entire checkout.
notes.measures: bounded timeouts, a circuit breaker and controlled retries. A slow carrier now only slows itself down.
